samples.summary: `Secure` is now silently dropped from session/refresh cookies (and `__Host-` from the state cookies) on any production deployment whose GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL is `http://` — including TLS-terminating-proxy setups the self-hosting guide itself instructs
samples.evidence: Before this change `AuthController.baseCookieOptions()` set `secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production'`. It now calls `useSecureCookies()` → `isSecureCookie()`, which at oauth-state.ts:193 returns **false** for any `http://` callback URL, ahead of the NODE_ENV fallback at :194. `packages/documentation/developers/self-hosting.md:123` still tells operators to set the GitHub Authorization callback URL to `http://your-domain:3000/auth/github/callback`, and a TLS-terminating edge in front of an `http://` backend is the ordinary self-hosted shape. Such a deployment, on upgrading, has `wafflebase_session` and `wafflebase_refresh` (both carrying full access/refresh JWTs, auth.controller.ts:335/343) emitted WITHOUT `Secure`, and the OAuth/CLI state and confirm cookies lose the `__Host-` prefix (oauth-state.ts:61) that the same file's comments call 'the only thing that stops a sibling subdomain from planting the browser's half of the double submit'. Attack: a network attacker (or any page able to force one plaintext `http://<host>/...` subresource) now receives the session JWT in the clear, and a foothold on any sibling subdomain regains cookie-tossing against the double-submit state. The only mitigation is the opt-in `COOKIE_SECURE=true`, and the warning the README promises for exactly this case does not exist in the code (see separate finding). Erring toward `false` here is the unsafe direction: an https origin that wrongly gets `secure:false` leaks a live session, whereas an http origin that wrongly gets `secure:true` merely fails to log in.

samples.summary: README and the self-hosting guide document a `400 Command-line sign-in requires an https server` refusal that exists nowhere in the backend; on plain-http deployments the CLI consent gate is in fact open and operators are told it is closed
samples.evidence: packages/backend/README.md:119-122 and packages/documentation/developers/self-hosting.md:126-130 both state that CLI sign-in 'answers `400 Command-line sign-in requires an https server` on a plain-http origin that is not loopback, because its consent gate is a cookie that anything on such an origin can plant.' No such check exists: `GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate` (github-auth.guard.ts:108-135) only runs `assertCliStartNotCrossSite`, and `CliLoginConfirmMiddleware.use` (cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:110-161) has no scheme/host test at all. On a plain-http non-loopback deployment `isSecureCookie()` returns false, so `wafflebase_cli_confirm` is set without `Secure` and without `__Host-` — precisely the cookie the docs say can be planted — and `?mode=cli` proceeds normally. An attacker with a foothold on the origin (or a network position, since the origin is cleartext) can plant the confirm cookie, compute `cliConfirmToken(plantedSecret, port, nonce, challenge)` themselves (the HMAC key is the cookie value they chose), and satisfy the gate for a `?mode=cli&port=<attacker port>` link, defeating the whole consent defence. Searched: grep for 'https server', 'Command-line sign-in', 'COOKIE_SECURE', 'useSecureCookies', 'isSecureCookie' across packages/backend/src; read github-auth.guard.ts, cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts, auth.controller.ts, auth.module.ts, main.ts in full.

samples.summary: `OAUTH_STATE_SECRET` and the HKDF-derived key it claims to replace do not exist in the code — the web OAuth state is an unkeyed SHA-256, so an operator who sets this variable gets no effect while believing the state key is decoupled from JWT_SECRET
samples.evidence: docs/design/backend.md:708 adds an env-var row: '`OAUTH_STATE_SECRET` | No | HKDF of `JWT_SECRET` | Key the OAuth login bindings are signed with … set it to an independent value to remove any relation between the `state` an unauthenticated `GET /auth/github` publishes and the session-signing key', and packages/backend/README.md:25-33 repeats it. Grepping the whole repo for `OAUTH_STATE_SECRET`, `hkdf`, and `bindingSecret` returns matches only in docs and docs/tasks lesson files — no source file reads either. The actual mechanism is `createWebOAuthState()` (oauth-state.ts:120-123), which is `secret = randomBytes(32)`, `state = 'web.' + sha256(secret)` — unkeyed, no HMAC, no derived key. So the documented knob is inert: an operator who sets `OAUTH_STATE_SECRET` to satisfy a hardening requirement changes nothing, and the design doc misdescribes the security property of the state binding to future reviewers. Searched: grep -i 'OAUTH_STATE_SECRET|hkdf|bindingSecret' across the repo; read oauth-state.ts, cli-auth.store.ts, auth.service usage of state, github-auth.guard.ts.

samples.summary: The launch-token indirection does not protect the nonce/PKCE challenge from the adversary it names: the loopback launch URL it puts in argv is itself a bearer credential any local user can dereference
samples.evidence: login.ts:326-331 and docs/design/cli.md ('The authorization URL never reaches argv or a log … opening a URL puts it in a child process's argv, which any local user can read (`ps`, `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`) on exactly the shared host these bindings are for, so `open()` is handed `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/launch/<32-byte token>` instead'). But the loopback listener is bound to 127.0.0.1 (login.ts:790) and 127.0.0.1 is reachable by *every* local user, not just the owner. A different-user local attacker reads the opener's argv, GETs `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/launch/<token>`, and the handler at login.ts:647-659 hands back a 302 whose `Location` is the full authorization URL — nonce and PKCE challenge included. They can then start their own GitHub login against the same nonce/challenge and push the resulting code at the victim's callback port, which accepts it because it carries the matching nonce (login.ts:720), fixating the victim's CLI onto the attacker's account. Single use only makes the theft noisy (the real browser then gets the 410 page at :670), it does not prevent it. The residual risk is acknowledged in one code comment but the design doc and the surrounding comments state the property as absolute, which is how a reader concludes this threat is closed.

samples.summary: The README promises a warning for the `NODE_ENV=production` + plain-http-callback cookie downgrade; no such warning is emitted anywhere, so the downgrade is entirely silent
samples.evidence: packages/backend/README.md:68-70 ('`NODE_ENV=production` with a non-loopback `http://` callback URL logs a warning for that reason') and packages/documentation/developers/self-hosting.md:137-138 ('logs a warning at the first login for this reason'). `isSecureCookie()` (oauth-state.ts:184-195) is a pure function with no logger, and grepping backend src for GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL shows only oauth-state.ts:189 and github.strategy.ts:46 — neither warns. This is the only operator-facing signal the docs offer for the `Secure`/`__Host-` downgrade described in the first finding, so its absence is what makes that downgrade silent on upgrade. Searched: grep 'GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL' across packages/**/*.ts; grep 'logs a warning'; read oauth-state.ts, github.strategy.ts, main.ts, app.module.ts.
searchedFor: grep 'logs a warning' in docs and packages

samples.summary: `COOKIE_SECURE=false`/`0` disables `Secure` and `__Host-` on every session and login cookie even on an https production deployment, and any other spelling is silently ignored rather than rejected
samples.evidence: isSecureCookie() at oauth-state.ts:185-187 honours `false`/`0` as an unconditional override, ahead of both the callback-URL scheme and NODE_ENV. No documented use case needs the negative direction — README:63-67 only describes `COOKIE_SECURE=true` — so the `false` branch exists purely as a footgun: one stray env var strips `Secure` from `wafflebase_session`/`wafflebase_refresh` and drops the `__Host-` prefix that the module's own comments call the sole defence against sibling-subdomain cookie tossing, with no warning. Relatedly, a value such as `yes`/`on`/`True!` falls through to the callback-URL branch silently, so a misconfigured operator believes `Secure` is forced when it is not.

samples.summary: `login-url.txt` is written with a follow-symlink `writeFileSync` after an `rmSync`, leaving a TOCTOU window in which the live login URL can be written through an attacker-planted symlink
samples.evidence: announceLoginUrl (login.ts:140-152) does `mkdirSync(dirname(file), {recursive:true})` — creating the directory with the default 0777&~umask (0755, not 0700) — then `rmSync(file, {force:true})` and `writeFileSync(file, url, {mode: 0o600})`. `writeFileSync` opens with `'w'`, which follows symlinks and ignores `mode` on an existing target. Between the rm and the write, anything that can create entries in that directory can plant `login-url.txt` as a symlink and receive the authorization URL (nonce + PKCE challenge) at a path of its choosing, with permissions of its choosing. Under the default `~/.wafflebase` only the owner can win that race, but `WAFFLEBASE_CONFIG` can point the config anywhere (the tests in this diff point it at `os.tmpdir()`), and a shared/CI checkout directory is exactly the headless, non-TTY case this file exists for. `flag: 'wx'` (O_EXCL) after the unlink would close it.

samples.summary: A `?mode=cli` start with an out-of-range port still falls through to a full browser login (issuing real session cookies), contradicting the fix this change's own lessons file records as done
samples.evidence: docs/tasks/active/20260812-cli-login-loopback-binding-lessons.md (added by this diff) states: "`port` kept an `if (valid) { … }` whose else-branch fell through to the browser login, so an unusable port issued the person real session cookies for a sign-in they had asked to hand to a terminal" — listed among the round-3 fixes. The code does not implement it: cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:118-122 returns `next()` when `parseCliPort` yields undefined, and github-auth.guard.ts:116 then takes the `else` branch and mints a *web* state, so `GET /auth/github?mode=cli&port=80` skips the confirmation page entirely and ends with `wafflebase_session`/`wafflebase_refresh` set on the browser. The cross-site check still runs, so this is confusion/consent-mismatch rather than a code-delivery bypass, but a reader of the lessons file would conclude the fall-through was closed.

verdict.reason: The documented refusal does not exist anywhere in the backend. Repo-wide grep for "Command-line" (excluding node_modules) yields only the two doc lines plus the confirm page's prose; no scheme or loopback test appears on any path reaching GET /auth/github?mode=cli. The only middleware registered ahead of that route is CliLoginConfirmMiddleware (auth.module.ts:45-49), whose use() (cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:110-161) branches solely on the confirm token vs cookie HMAC; GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate (github-auth.guard.ts:108-135) adds only assertCliStartNotCrossSite, a Sec-Fetch-Site check that returns early when the header is absent (line 173). Enumerating every non-spec throw in packages/backend/src/auth produces no scheme-related error, and grepping req.secure/x-forwarded-proto/protocol/scheme across packages/backend/src finds only isSecureCookie() (oauth-state.ts:184-195), which downgrades the cookie rather than refusing the flow. Consequently on a plain-http non-loopback deployment wafflebase_cli_confirm is set without Secure and without the __Host- prefix (cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:55-68 with hostPrefixedCookieName, oauth-state.ts:60-62), so an attacker with a foothold on (or network position over) the cleartext origin can plant the cookie, compute cliConfirmToken with the secret they chose (cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:96-106), and satisfy the consent gate for an attacker-chosen ?mode=cli&port= link. The docs telling operators the gate is closed makes this a real, unmitigated weakening of the CLI consent gate, which falls in the authorization/access-control lane; the parallel doc claim of a first-login warning is also absent (auth.controller.ts has no Logger/warn). I found no counterexample.

verdict.reason: The absence itself is real: docs/design/backend.md:708 and packages/backend/README.md:25-34 document OAUTH_STATE_SECRET as an HKDF-of-JWT_SECRET signing key, and no source file reads it (repo-wide grep for OAUTH_STATE_SECRET, STATE_SECRET, hkdf, and dynamic process.env[...] lookups matches only docs, README and .agent-review artifacts). But the security harm the finding asserts does not exist, because the property the knob claims to provide is already unconditionally guaranteed. Every OAuth binding key is fresh CSPRNG material with no relation to JWT_SECRET: web state is sha256(randomBytes(32)) (oauth-state.ts:120-123) verified constant-time (oauth-state.ts:132-140); the CLI state token and its csrf are both randomBytes(32) with only sha256(csrf) stored and compared constant-time (cli-auth.store.ts:59-62,104); and the CLI confirm token is an HMAC keyed by a per-request randomBytes(32) cookie secret, explicitly documented as having no server key to configure (cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:89-106,152-154). JWT_SECRET is used only for JWT signing (auth.service.ts:51, jwt.strategy.ts:18). So an operator setting the variable is already in the hardened state and no false sense of security yields exploitability; oauth-state.ts:38-41 further documents why an HMAC over the double-submit secret would add nothing, the __Host- write restriction (oauth-state.ts:49-62) being the load-bearing control. The residual defect is documentation accuracy, which belongs to the docs/design-fit lens and is already recorded there (.agent-review/design-fit/verdict.json:32-33); it is not a missing gate, secret exposure, injection, weak randomness, or broken crypto check, and no attacker action is enabled by any cited line.

verdict.reason: The finding is accurate as described. `armLaunch` (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:815-819) returns `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/launch/<token>` and that value is handed to `deps.openBrowser()` at login.ts:340, so a bearer credential still lands in the opener child's argv — the very exposure the comment at login.ts:325-331 and docs/design/cli.md:226-231 claim to have eliminated ("The authorization URL never reaches argv or a log"). The listener binds 127.0.0.1 (login.ts:790), which is reachable by every local uid, and the handler at login.ts:643-659 answers a matching token with a 302 whose `Location` is the full authorization URL built at login.ts:333, carrying both the nonce and the PKCE challenge. Those two values are exactly what the victim's callback then trusts: login.ts:711-728 accepts any callback echoing the nonce, and the in-process verifier from createPkcePair (login.ts:426-432) matches the stolen challenge, so a code minted by an attacker's own GitHub login against the same nonce/challenge/port is redeemable by the victim in fetchLoginSession, fixating the CLI onto the attacker's account. No guard makes this unreachable: single use (login.ts:650) and the 410 page (login.ts:670-677) only make a win noisy, and on a headless host openBrowser (login.ts:107-115) cannot tell "spawned" from "opened", so an undereferenced token stays live for the full 5-minute CALLBACK_TIMEOUT_MS (login.ts:505). In-lane as sensitive-data exposure enabling login/session fixation; no refutation ground applies.

finding.summary: The session and refresh cookies still carry no `__Host-`/`__Secure-` prefix, so even with `secureCookies()===true` a sibling subdomain can plant `wafflebase_session`/`wafflebase_refresh` — the protection the new comment claims for 'a cookie worth stealing' covers only the `Secure` flag
finding.evidence: `baseCookieOptions` (auth.controller.ts:534-538) returns `{httpOnly, secure, sameSite}` and `setAuthCookies` writes the fixed names `wafflebase_session` / `wafflebase_refresh` (lines 59-60, 484, 492) with no prefix and no `path`. Grep for `__Host-` across packages shows the prefix is applied only in `loginCookieName` (github-auth.guard.ts:238); no session cookie ever gets it. The guard's own reasoning (github-auth.guard.ts:222-232) is that without the prefix any sibling subdomain or anything able to inject a `Set-Cookie` for the registrable domain can write the cookie — applied to the session cookie that is session fixation: an attacker plants their own valid access/refresh token, the victim's browser sends it on every request, and the victim's work lands in the attacker's account. This delta's new comment (lines 527-533) asserts the session cookie's exposure is now handled by `COOKIE_SECURE` + the warning, which addresses only the transport flag, not cookie planting. Pre-existing code, raised because the delta reasons explicitly about this cookie's threat model.

verdict.reason: The absence claim holds. `ACCESS_COOKIE_NAME`/`REFRESH_COOKIE_NAME` are the bare literals `wafflebase_session`/`wafflebase_refresh` (auth.controller.ts:35-36), written by `setAuthCookies` (auth.controller.ts:335,343) with `baseCookieOptions()` (auth.controller.ts:366-376) which sets only httpOnly/secure/sameSite — no `__Host-`/`__Secure-` prefix and no `path`. A repo-wide grep (excluding node_modules) shows the prefix helper does exist but is applied only to the OAuth/CLI state cookies (oauth-state.ts:61, consumed by cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:39,58,63); no session-cookie path ever reaches it. There is no compensating control: `jwt.strategy.ts:13` reads `request.cookies.wafflebase_session` and `validate` (jwt.strategy.ts:22-32) checks only signature and `tokenType==='access'`, with no binding to the browser that obtained the token, and main.ts:64 is a plain `cookieParser()`. The names are not env-configurable and there is no other setter or proxy rewriting them. So an attacker with a sibling subdomain (or any ability to inject Set-Cookie for the registrable domain) can plant their own valid access/refresh JWT in the victim's browser — session fixation, exactly the threat the repo's own oauth-state.ts:23-61 and oauth-state.spec.ts:53-97 cite as the reason for `__Host-` on the state cookies. The reviewer's line numbers are stale (534-538, github-auth.guard.ts:238 do not match this tree) but the substantive claim is verified at the locations above. In-lane (auth/session integrity) and major: a clear weakness requiring an adjacent-subdomain or cookie-injection foothold rather than a standalone exploit.
